hook_text: Your wall socket says 220 volts. It has never once been 220 volts. Here's the truth.
clip_script: Find an old bicycle with a dynamo — the little knurled cylinder that tilts against the tyre — and you are holding a complete power station. Pedal, and the headlamp lights. Sprint, and it brightens. Crack the casing open and the inventory is almost embarrassing: one magnet, one coil of wire. That, plus your legs, is the whole technology. And the payment is real: engage the dynamo and pedalling stiffens noticeably — that extra effort in your calves IS the lamplight, energy conservation auditing every pedal stroke. Scale it up and you have national infrastructure: in a power station the rider is replaced by steam, falling water or wind, and the coil weighs as much as a truck — but the physics does not change one letter. Motion in, electricity out, and the current naturally sloshes to-and-fro as the coil spins: AC is just what rotation sounds like in electrical form. Now the socket confession. The 220 on your wall is never actually there — the voltage sprints up to plus 311, dives to minus 311, fifty round trips a second. So why 220? Because your kettle heats on the forward stroke AND the backward stroke — heat follows current squared — and 220 is the steady voltage that would cook exactly as fast as the wave does. Peak for the engineers. Rms for your bill. One spinning coil behind it all.
visual_style: A bicycle dynamo cut open into magnet and coil, morphing into a turbine hall; a sine wave sprinting between plus and minus 311 with a steady 220 line glowing through its middle; a kettle heating on both strokes of a sloshing current.
mood: Wonder at scale — the same humble trick from bicycle lamp to national grid.
pacing: Dynamo-in-the-hand opener, legs-pay-for-light beat, scale-up sweep, socket confession, rms reveal.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and own every generator, motor and rms question in your final exams.
